lesson.title: Reading a Sign Chart Like a Detective: Crossing Zero vs. Touching Zero
lesson.summary: Sign change analysis is the habit of testing an actual point in every region a sign chart creates rather than assuming the signs simply alternate, since a zero from an even-power factor only touches zero without crossing it, a distinction that becomes essential once the same technique is applied to f prime and f double prime.
lesson.body:
A sign chart divides the number line at the zeros and undefined points of a function, then records whether the function is positive or negative on each resulting piece. It is tempting to assume the sign simply alternates from piece to piece, plus, minus, plus, minus, but that shortcut breaks down whenever a zero comes from a repeated factor. The safe method is always to plug an actual test point from each region back into the function and check the sign directly, never to guess based on a pattern.

Consider h(x) = (x + 1)^2 (x - 3). Setting h(x) = 0 gives zeros at x = -1 and x = 3. Test one point from each of the three regions the two zeros create. At x = -2: h(-2) = (-2 + 1)^2 (-2 - 3) = (1)(-5) = -5, negative. At x = 0: h(0) = (0 + 1)^2 (0 - 3) = (1)(-3) = -3, also negative. At x = 4: h(4) = (4 + 1)^2 (4 - 3) = (25)(1) = 25, positive.

Notice what happened at x = -1: the sign was negative just to the left of it and negative just to the right of it too, so h does not actually change sign there. That happens because the factor (x + 1) is squared, an even power, so (x + 1)^2 can never go negative, it only touches zero and bounces back to the same sign it had before. At x = 3, on the other hand, the sign flips cleanly from negative to positive, because the factor (x - 3) appears to an odd power, the first power, so it genuinely crosses through zero. The rule that generalizes from this example is: a zero coming from a factor raised to an even power only touches the axis, no sign change, while a zero coming from a factor raised to an odd power crosses the axis, a genuine sign change. Keep this distinction close at hand. The Second Derivative Test and the search for inflection points both hinge on exactly this kind of sign change analysis applied to f'' instead of a generic function, and a value where f'' equals zero will turn out to matter only if the sign of f'' genuinely flips there, not merely touches zero.
